content: 1. The regulation of prosthetic and orthotic products is essential to ensure access to safe, effective, and high-quality devices. These products, being integral to healthcare, require a regulatory framework that encompasses not only the final products but also the components and materials used in their manufacture. This framework should be embedded within the national healthcare regulatory system. 2. Structural testing of prosthetic and orthotic components and materials is necessary to confirm compliance with ISO or equivalent standards. This ensures that the products are strong, durable, and safe for use. Additionally, clinical field tests can be conducted to verify that these products are fit for their intended purpose. 3. The use of nationally or internationally recognized scientific testing methods ensures the reliability, validity, and comparability of results on a global scale. 4. National regulation of prosthetic and orthotic products, components, and materials should be an integral part of the national healthcare regulatory system. 5. Prosthetic and orthotic products must undergo structural testing to ensure compliance with ISO or equivalent standards before being introduced to the market. 6. Technical and clinical research and innovation are critical for advancing prosthetics and orthotics. More evidence on the cost-effectiveness and quality of treatments and products will help make appropriate services accessible to a larger population in need. 7. There is a significant lack of evidence regarding the appropriateness of technologies and methods, as well as the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of treatments in the prosthetics and orthotics sector. Increased national and international research efforts are needed to improve both practice and services. 8. A major limitation in the field is the insufficient training of prosthetists and orthotists to conduct research. Organizations and higher education institutions should encourage and facilitate research while training professionals to conduct studies and disseminate findings. 9. To increase access to prosthetic and orthotic services in resource-limited settings, new, affordable products and methods are required. These should be mass-produced with cost-effectiveness, quality control, and contextual appropriateness in mind. 10. Despite advancements in research and development, the availability of prosthetic and orthotic products has not significantly improved for most individuals in lowand middle-income countries. 11. Governments are responsible for ensuring the availability of new products at affordable costs. However, this can only be achieved through collaboration with national and international stakeholders, including private industry and targeted international funding. 12. Clinical and technical research in prosthetics and orthotics should be conducted, and the results should be shared both nationally and globally. 13. Affordable prosthetic and orthotic products that are cost-effective, of good quality, and context-appropriate should be developed and made widely available. 14. Personnel providing prosthetic and orthotic services include professionals, associates, and assistants, with roles divided into clinicians (prosthetists and/or orthotists and their associates) and non-clinicians (technicians and support staff). They work collaboratively with healthcare, rehabilitation, and administrative teams to provide treatment for individuals with various physical impairments or functional limitations. 15. There is a global shortage of prosthetics and orthotics personnel. The provision of high-quality prostheses and orthoses depends on the availability of competent, adequately trained clinicians, non-clinicians, and other healthcare personnel. 16. While many individuals with physical impairments can be treated by prosthetics and orthotics personnel alone, those with severe or complex health problems often require interventions from a multidisciplinary team of healthcare and rehabilitation professionals. 17. Multidisciplinary teamwork is essential in rehabilitation, including prosthetics and orthotics, as it ensures timely and effective treatment. 18. Prosthetics and orthotics services should be provided by competent, adequately trained professionals. 19. Complex prosthetic and orthotic treatments and care for complicated cases should be managed by a multidisciplinary team of professionals with complementary skills. 20. Structured training and continuing professional development (CPD) are essential for building the capacity of prosthetics and orthotics personnel. Other healthcare and social care personnel also require knowledge of prosthetics and orthotics, depending on their roles and involvement in the field. 21. Despite the expansion of training programs in prosthetics and orthotics over the past three decades, the demand for personnel continues to exceed the supply. Transformative training and education are needed to address this gap. 22. Training in prosthetics and orthotics should align with national and international educational standards and be available at various levels to meet national needs fully. 23. All healthcare and allied health personnel should have a basic understanding of prosthetics and orthotics to identify and refer individuals for treatment and coordinate care effectively. 24. Continuing professional development (CPD) opportunities are severely lacking, particularly in resource-poor settings. CPD is crucial for maintaining and improving the quality of services provided by professionals at all levels. 25. CPD allows experienced personnel with limited formal training to update their knowledge and skills, maximizing their motivation and capacity. Prosthetics and orthotics personnel have a duty to engage in CPD, and workplaces should foster a stimulating learning environment. 26. Workforce planning is essential for effective prosthetics and orthotics services. It involves determining the demand for personnel, comparing it with the existing supply, and assessing training needs. 27. Workforce planning should consider all disciplines required in prosthetics and orthotics services at all levels. Each service delivery unit should have at least one experienced prosthetist and/or orthotist to supervise and guide clinical and technical work. 28. Strategies are needed to retain prosthetics and orthotics professionals, ensuring they remain motivated and engaged in service delivery, even in rural and remote settings. 29. Professional regulation and recognition are necessary for prosthetists and orthotists to enforce accountability and reduce the risk of harm to users. Recognition enhances motivation, retention, and professional development, ultimately improving service provision. 30. Prosthetists and orthotists should be regulated by the state within the framework of health professional regulations. They should assume responsibility for services provided by associate and non-clinical personnel under their supervision. 31. Prosthetics and orthotics personnel should have a clear career structure and employment conditions aligned with those of other health professionals. Proper classification of these professionals is an incentive, offering increased opportunities for promotion.
